Summary
Autism diagnostic instruments developed and validated mainly in children do not transfer consistently to adults because symptom expression, cognitive profiles, and diagnostic frameworks change across development, and measurement tools are tuned to child-specific behaviors and language levels. These factors shift sensitivity and specificity and often require confirmatory, adult-appropriate instruments and clinical integration to maintain accuracy in adults. <cite id="77afbcf4-0">Standardized diagnostic tools like the ADI‑R and ADOS‑2 underpin clinical ASD diagnosis across ages, with adult and child versions of the SRS‑2 used together when needed</cite><cite id="9773065e-1">Adult assessment batteries include ADI‑R, SRS, 3Di‑Adult, and ADOS‑2 Module 4, reflecting that child-validated tools are not sufficient alone in late life</cite><cite id="9773065e-4">In real-world clinical cohorts, predictive values of common questionnaires are lower than in general-population research settings</cite><cite id="738221c9-4">Comparative performance depends on setting, and retrospective knowledge at testing can bias accuracy</cite>.

Why accuracy is inconsistent: key mechanisms
1) Developmental changes in symptom domains and expression
Across childhood to adulthood, social reciprocity and pragmatic communication often attenuate with typical language and social learning, while restricted/repetitive behaviors (RRBs) and attentional/rigid behaviors can persist; standardized tools are calibrated around developmental milestones, so items and thresholds may misfit adults. <cite id="3677c33b-0">DSM‑5 combined social interaction and communication into a single criterion and consolidated Asperger’s and PDD‑NOS under ASD, simplifying categories but obscuring age‑specific trajectories</cite><cite id="3677c33b-1">Longitudinal “best‑estimate” reclassifications show that diagnostic formulations can shift slightly across DSM eras, and separating language level and intellectual ability is crucial to interpret core features over time</cite><cite id="738221c9-2">In an adult ASD sample, ADOS‑2 and ADI‑R cutoffs aligned with calibrated severity, underscoring the need to adjust for age and language level</cite>. In practice, adult triage therefore uses questionnaires (AQ/SRS‑2) followed by ADOS/ADI confirmation to capture behaviors that may not be salient or accessible in retrospective self‑reports. <cite id="9773065e-0">Adults are commonly screened with AQ and SRS‑2 and then confirmed with ADOS‑2 using DSM‑5 criteria</cite>.

2) Diagnostic drift and retrospective bias
Adults are diagnosed under DSM‑5’s unified ASD category, whereas many had prior labels (e.g., Asperger’s, PDD‑NOS) or self‑identify based on adult‑era concepts; applying child‑validated instruments across these shifting constructs can misclassify or dilute profiles. <cite id="3677c33b-0">DSM‑5’s merging of Asperger’s/PDD‑NOS into ASD and combining social interaction/communication criteria complicate cross‑age measurement alignment</cite><cite id="3677c33b-1">Over decades, small shifts in diagnostic formulations are observed; separating verbal/nonverbal abilities and language level is essential, as these factors affect observed symptom patterns</cite><cite id="738221c9-4">In adult assessment, if individuals already suspect ASD, self‑report can be biased by prior diagnosis and expectation; predictive values vary widely by setting and questionnaire</cite>. Adult‑specific cautions also emphasize requiring corroborating signs and external informants to counteract self‑diagnosis and attenuated presentation. <cite id="3677c33b-4">For adults, adding an external informant and requiring atypical signs consistent with developmental history improves diagnostic reasoning when relying on DSM‑5’s broad spectrum</cite>.

3) Cognitive confounds: IQ, language level, and ceiling effects
Child instruments often embed age- and language-normed items and calibrated algorithms; in adults, variable IQ, language proficiency, and verbal‑nonverbal discrepancies can distort scores. <cite id="77afbcf4-3">ADOS/ADI severity scores are calibrated to age and language level; CSS was used to index symptom severity relative to these levels</cite><cite id="9773065e-0">Clinical pipelines explicitly stratify adults by IQ and use ADOS‑2 thresholds with DSM‑5 confirmation to mitigate misclassification</cite>. Ceiling effects and item content focused on school/childhood contexts can inflate false‑positive or false‑negative clustering in adults with average language who show attenuated social reciprocity but preserved RRBs. <cite id="738221c9-1">SRS‑2 extends into adulthood but relies on an unchanged item set from 4–18 years; factor structure and measurement invariance must be tested across age and reporter, because factor loadings and thresholds can shift across major developmental intervals</cite>. Adult‑adapted tools and cutoffs (e.g., ADOS Module 4, RAADS‑R) improve alignment by targeting adult communication modes and broader phenotype ranges. <cite id="9773065e-1">ADOS‑2 Module 4 and adult interview/adapted questionnaires are recommended for adults</cite><cite id="9773065e-2">RAADS‑R shows 97% sensitivity and 100% specificity against ADI/ADOS/DSM‑IV criteria with high test–retest reliability, illustrating gains from adult‑specific validation</cite>.

Adult populations include late‑diagnosed individuals, co‑occurring intellectual disability, neurodevelopmental disorders, and age‑related comorbidities (e.g., mental health conditions, dementia risk), which shift instrument performance relative to child samples. <cite id="9773065e-1">In older adults, differentiating lifelong autistic traits from new or aggravated symptoms (e.g., dementia) is critical when interpreting assessment results</cite><cite id="3677c33b-0">NICE guidance notes that measures used in adults since DSM‑5 should align to the updated criteria and comorbidity framework</cite><cite id="3677c33b-2">Exclusion of participants with IQ <85 and co‑occurring genetic syndromes in some ASD samples highlights that lower IQ thresholds and comorbidity strata affect observed instrument performance</cite>. Child‑focused language, school contexts, and social play content may not map cleanly to adult life domains; measurement invariance is often violated across child→adult transitions. <cite id="738221c9-1">SRS‑2’s factor structure and invariance must be evaluated across age (child vs adult), sex, and reporter; age‑related changes and informant differences imply that items may load differently and thresholds may be misaligned when moving from child to adult samples</cite>. Adult versions attempt to address this by providing self‑ and other‑report adaptations and updated norms, yet still face ceiling effects in high‑functioning adults and sensitivity to rater dynamics. <cite id="77afbcf4-0">Adult and child SRS‑2 scores can be merged due to compatible item distributions, but this does not guarantee invariant interpretation across ages</cite><cite id="9773065e-1">3Di‑Adult and ADOS‑2 Module 4 target adult communication and behavior to improve construct alignment</cite>.

Adult‑validated tools explicitly address developmental invariance and comorbidity contexts:
- ADOS‑2 and ADI‑R with adult modules and calibrated algorithms; ADOS severity calibrated to age/language level improves discrimination in adults. <cite id="77afbcf4-3">Calibrated severity scores adjust for age/language; autism severity across adult age bands did not differ within ASD, suggesting robustness after calibration</cite><cite id="9773065e-1">ADOS‑2 Module 4 and adult interview forms evaluate verbal and nonverbal behaviors suitable for adults</cite>.

- Staged, confirmatory pipelines: <cite id="9773065e-0">Adults are often triaged with AQ/SRS‑2 and then confirmed with ADOS‑2 and expert clinical opinion under DSM‑5</cite>. Even when adult scales screen positive, many adults require ADOS/ADI confirmation to reach a threshold; conversely, some adults with ASD do not meet adult questionnaire cutoffs but exceed ADOS severity thresholds. <cite id="9773065e-0">Three autistic adults did not meet AQ/SRS‑2 cutoffs yet scored >7 on ADOS‑2, prompting diagnosis via clinical consensus</cite>.

- Use age‑ and language‑appropriate algorithms and adult modules for ADOS/ADI; interpret SRS‑2 with attention to invariance and reporter choice. <cite id="77afbcf4-3">Calibrated severity (CSS) adjusts for age/language</cite><cite id="738221c9-1">SRS‑2 requires testing of factor invariance across age and reporter to ensure valid comparisons</cite>.
- Combine adult questionnaires with performance-based observation/interviews and clinical consensus; avoid relying solely on child-derived cutoffs in adults. <cite id="9773065e-1">Questionnaires are useful adjuncts but require clinical integration</cite><cite id="9773065e-0">Adult triage questionnaires are followed by ADOS‑2 confirmation and DSM‑5 review</cite>.
- Account for IQ and comorbidity explicitly; stratify by verbal/nonverbal IQ and consider late‑diagnosis and dementia risk. <cite id="3677c33b-1">Differentiating by language level and IQ is crucial to interpret diagnostic change over time</cite><cite id="9773065e-1">Interpreting autism traits alongside potential dementia requires historical context</cite>.
- Prefer adult‑validated instruments (e.g., RAADS‑R, 3Di‑Adult, ADOS‑2 Module 4) when available, and evaluate predictive values within the target adult clinical population rather than extrapolating from child research cohorts. <cite id="9773065e-2">Adult‑specific scales can approach near‑perfect sensitivity/specificity when validated against gold standards</cite><cite id="738221c9-4">Predictive values are highly setting‑specific and often lower in clinical practice than in research</cite>.
- Mitigate retrospective bias by incorporating external informants and developmental sign constancy, especially when individuals self‑refer or have sparse early histories. <cite id="3677c33b-4">Requiring atypical signs consistent with clinical development and adding external informants improves adult diagnostic reasoning under DSM‑5’s broad spectrum</cite>.

Bottom line
Child-focused autism instruments reflect developmentally specific behaviors and norms. In adults, changing cognitive profiles (IQ, language, comorbidity), diagnostic frameworks (DSM‑5 consolidation and retrospective reclassification), and symptom salience shift the operating point of these tools, producing inconsistent accuracy unless scores are recalibrated and complemented with adult-adapted measures and clinical consensus. <cite id="77afbcf4-3">Calibration for age/language level in ADOS/ADI is essential</cite><cite id="9773065e-1">Adult-adapted batteries (3Di‑Adult, ADOS‑2 Module 4) and questionnaires (SRS‑2, AQ) are commonly used</cite><cite id="9773065e-2">Adult-adapted scales like RAADS‑R can achieve high sensitivity and specificity with ADI/ADOS anchoring</cite><cite id="738221c9-4">Predictive values in adult clinical settings are often lower and setting‑specific, and retrospective knowledge biases results</cite><cite id="3677c33b-0">DSM‑5 category consolidation and domain merging complicate cross-age transfer</cite>. Title: Autism, Diagnostics, and Dementia: A Consensus Report From the 2nd International Summit on Intellectual Disabilities and Dementia
Snippet: A significant concern arises when autism is not diagnosed earlier in life, leaving older adults to navigate their symptoms without formal recognition. Title: The Predictive Value of the AQ and the SRS-A in the Diagnosis of ASD in Adults in Clinical Practice
Snippet: Questionnaires are widely used in autism assessment. However, their psychometric properties are generally not evaluated in clinical practice, and the comparability and applicability of such research is limited because questionnaires are often not simultaneously evaluated. This certainly pertains to predictive values which are highly population and setting specific. This study evaluated the power of AQ and SRS-A in predicting an ASD diagnosis within the same clinical population. The patient records of 92 adults, referred for autism assessment, were analyzed. The AQ proved somewhat better than the SRS-A at discriminating and predicting autism. The predictive values of both questionnaires were lower than reported in general population studies. Title: The Predictive Value of the AQ and the SRS-A in the Diagnosis of ASD in Adults in Clinical Practice
Snippet: Questionnaires are widely used in autism assessment. However, their psychometric properties are generally not evaluated in clinical practice, and the comparability and applicability of such research is limited because questionnaires are often not simultaneously evaluated. This certainly pertains to predictive values which are highly population and setting specific. This study evaluated the power of AQ and SRS-A in predicting an ASD diagnosis within the same clinical population. The patient records of 92 adults, referred for autism assessment, were analyzed. The AQ proved somewhat better than the SRS-A at discriminating and predicting autism. The predictive values of both questionnaires were lower than reported in general population studies. Psychometric results in core publications appear less representative for clinical practice.

Snippet: In practice, however, high sensitivity often comes at the expense of specificity, and vice versa. This also applies for PPV and NPV. Depending on the specific use of the questionnaire, a choice must be made concerning which values are to be assigned the most weight. 

Various ASD questionnaires for adults are used in clinical practice, including the Autism-spectrum Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al. 2001), the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R; Ritvo et al. 2011), the Social Responsiveness Scale Adult version (SRS-A; Constantino and Todd 2005), and the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ; Rutter et al. 2003). Of these instruments, the AQ and the SRS-A appear to be the most commonly used in the Netherlands. These questionnaires differ in several aspects, such as the length of the questionnaire (50 or fewer items for the AQ, as compared to 64 items for the SRS-A), the cost of the questionnaire (open source for the AQ, as opposed to paid for the SRS-A), the availability of standards (only a cut-off score for the AQ, whereas there are standardized scores available for the SRS-A) and the psychometric properties of these questionnaires, including the predictive values. Looking at the AQ, this questionnaire possesses satisfactory to good psychometric qualities (Baron-Cohen et al. 2001;Hoekstra et al. 2008). The sensitivity of the AQ is .79, and the specificity is .98 (with a cut-off value of 32; Baron-Cohen et al. 2001). When PPV and NPV are calculated with MedCalc (MedCalc Software, Belgium) for aforementioned studies, both values are .93. The SRS-A is the adult version of the SRS. The SRS has proven itself as a reliable questionnaire with good psychometric qualities when applied for detecting possible ASD in children (Bölte et al. 2008(Bölte et al. , 2011)). According to the Dutch professional manual, the adult version also has satisfactory psychometric qualities (Noens et al. 2012).

Snippet: It should be noted that, in the professional manuals and core publications for the AQ and SRS-A, patients were already aware of their ASD diagnoses at the time that they completed the questionnaire. 

To summarize, the predictive values of different questionnaires-in this case, their ability to predict a clinical ASD diagnosis-are difficult to compare over studies, since different settings and research groups are involved, as was illustrated in Table 1. In order to properly compare two questionnaires, they should be analyzed in the same setting and group. The present study is the first to compare the AQ and the SRS-A within the same clinical setting. There has been, however, one study within a non-clinical population of students, in which both were compared as screening instruments for the broader autism phenotype (people with ASD traits without a true ASD diagnosis, and thus with a very mild severity). In that study, the SRS-A had the strongest criterion validity (Ingersoll et al. 2011). The goal of the present study is to compare the value of both ASD questionnaires in correctly predicting the ASD diagnosis in a clinically suspected adult population. This may help in determining which questionnaire to use in the assessment phase for adults in mental healthcare.

Various ASD questionnaires for adults are used in clinical practice, including the Autism-spectrum Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al. 2001), the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R; Ritvo et al. 2011), the Social Responsiveness Scale Adult version (SRS-A; Constantino and Todd 2005), and the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ; Rutter et al. 2003). Of these instruments, the AQ and the SRS-A appear to be the most commonly used in the Netherlands. These questionnaires differ in several aspects, such as the length of the questionnaire (50 or fewer items for the AQ, as compared to 64 items for the SRS-A), the cost of the questionnaire (open source for the AQ, as opposed to paid for the SRS-A), the availability of standards (only a cut-off score for the AQ, whereas there are standardized scores available for the SRS-A) and the psychometric properties of these questionnaires, including the predictive values. Looking at the AQ, this questionnaire possesses satisfactory to good psychometric qualities (Baron-Cohen et al. 2001;Hoekstra et al. 2008). The sensitivity of the AQ is .79, and the specificity is .98 (with a cut-off value of 32; Baron-Cohen et al. 2001). When PPV and NPV are calculated with MedCalc (MedCalc Software, Belgium) for aforementioned studies, both values are .93. The SRS-A is the adult version of the SRS. The SRS has proven itself as a reliable questionnaire with good psychometric qualities when applied for detecting possible ASD in children (Bölte et al. 2008(Bölte et al. , 2011)). According to the Dutch professional manual, the adult version also has satisfactory psychometric qualities (Noens et al. 2012).

It should be noted that, in the professional manuals and core publications for the AQ and SRS-A, patients were already aware of their ASD diagnoses at the time that they completed the questionnaire. 

To summarize, the predictive values of different questionnaires-in this case, their ability to predict a clinical ASD diagnosis-are difficult to compare over studies, since different settings and research groups are involved, as was illustrated in Table 1. In order to properly compare two questionnaires, they should be analyzed in the same setting and group. The present study is the first to compare the AQ and the SRS-A within the same clinical setting. There has been, however, one study within a non-clinical population of students, in which both were compared as screening instruments for the broader autism phenotype (people with ASD traits without a true ASD diagnosis, and thus with a very mild severity). In that study, the SRS-A had the strongest criterion validity (Ingersoll et al. 2011). The goal of the present study is to compare the value of both ASD questionnaires in correctly predicting the ASD diagnosis in a clinically suspected adult population. This may help in determining which questionnaire to use in the assessment phase for adults in mental healthcare.

documents.snippet: Questionnaires are widely used in autism assessment. However, their psychometric properties are generally not evaluated in clinical practice, and the comparability and applicability of such research is limited because questionnaires are often not simultaneously evaluated. This certainly pertains to predictive values which are highly population and setting specific. This study evaluated the power of AQ and SRS-A in predicting an ASD diagnosis within the same clinical population. The patient records of 92 adults, referred for autism assessment, were analyzed. The AQ proved somewhat better than the SRS-A at discriminating and predicting autism. The predictive values of both questionnaires were lower than reported in general population studies. Psychometric results in core publications appear less representative for clinical practice.
